snippets.snippet_text: The Hebrew word for 'double portion' (pi shenayim, literally 'a mouth of two') is the legal formula for inheritance in Deuteronomy 21:17—the firstborn son's privilege. When Elisha asks for this from Elijah, he's using covenant law to claim not just succession, but the fullness of prophetic authority.

The Jordan River crossing by Elijah and Elisha echoes Joshua's crossing on dry ground—but with a crucial difference. The mantle (aderet) becomes the instrument of power, connecting the prophet's authority to the ancient temple's waters and the washing/anointing that mark covenantal entry into new realms.

When Elisha strikes the Jordan with the mantle and cries 'Where is the LORD God of Elijah?'—the verb ayyeh ('where?') in prophetic speech isn't asking a literal question. It's a demand for divine presence and manifestation, claiming the same power that parted the waters for his predecessor.

Elisha's healing of Jericho's water happens at the motza (source/outlet)—not downstream. The principle: healing begins at the source. He uses salt in a new vessel, invoking the 'covenant of salt' (Numbers 18:19), making the miracle a covenantal restoration, not just a temporary fix.

The widow with the oil jar has only one jar—but Elisha tells her to borrow vessels from neighbors. The miracle multiplies in proportion to her faith and community trust. In temple language, she presents herself as a 'clean vessel' ready to receive abundance, mirroring the anointing principle of consecration.

The Shunammite woman's promise of a son uses the phrase 'at the season of life' (ka-et chayyah)—the exact language from Sarah's promise in Genesis 18. Both barren women, both promises of impossible conception, both given by divine representatives. This parallel echoes across centuries of covenant faithfulness.
